hardware.name: NVIDIA DGX Spark
hardware.note: torch.cuda.get_arch_list() on this part returns sm_80/90/100/110/120 -- nothing is built for 12.1. Documented consequences on vLLM specifically: FLASHINFER_CUTLASS for NVFP4 MoE was removed on sm_121 'and it costs 13%'; HUMMING cannot initialize; VLLM_CUTLASS and FLASHINFER_TRTLLM fail with 'kernel does not support current device'. That gap is the prize.

substrate.why: vLLM on this fleet is a pip wheel with precompiled CUDA extensions (_C_stable_libtorch.abi3.so, _flashmla_C.abi3.so, ...). Nobody has built it from source on aarch64/GB10, so there is no vendored tree to edit. Submissions are Python patches applied over the installed wheel.

wheel.note: Pinned exactly. A different wheel is a different substrate and its scores are not comparable.

substrate.mechanism: A submission is a directory under patches/<name>/ containing sitecustomize.py. It is put on PYTHONPATH for the candidate arm only, so it applies at interpreter startup and therefore reaches vLLM's spawned engine and worker processes -- which a post-import monkeypatch would not. Precedent: bench/patches/laguna-int4 on howtospark forces the Triton MoE path over Marlin in four lines.
substrate.outOfScope: CUDA kernels in csrc/. Reaching them needs a from-source vLLM build for sm_121, which does not exist yet on this hardware and is tracked as its own milestone -- it is also what would unlock recovering the documented 13%.

editableSurface.rule: patches/<name>/**. Nothing else may differ between the arms: same wheel, same model file, same serve arguments, same environment apart from PYTHONPATH.
editableSurface.enforcement: The harness builds both arms from the target's own serveArgs and diffs the wheel version and model sha256. A submission that changes the serve command is changing the measurement, not the engine.

gates.rule: Wheel version, model file sha256 and serve arguments are byte-identical between arms. Only PYTHONPATH differs.
Candidate output is byte-identical to the baseline arm on the target's prompts, at batch 1, warm, under the pinned serve config.
On prompts generated fresh from a random seed: output identical AND the speedup reproduces within tolerance.
gates.whySpeedupToo: THIS IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS HERE, and it is stricter than the llama.cpp arena's gate 3. There, the editable surface is CUDA kernels, so a submission physically cannot memoize a response. Here the submission is arbitrary Python: a patch could cache completions keyed on the prompt and return byte-identical tokens at absurd speed, passing gates 1, 2 and 4 cleanly. Freshly generated prompts break that -- a cache cannot hit an input nobody has seen -- but only if the held-out arm is TIMED as well as compared. Identity alone would let the cheat through.
gates.toleranceNote: The held-out decode speedup must be at least this fraction of the claimed speedup's excess over 1.0. A real engine-level win generalizes to unseen prompts; a lookup table does not.

gates.rule: score > the current leaderboard score for every target claimed.

scoring.pairing: Paired ratios, arms alternating in one session on one node.

pinnedServeConfig.why: vLLM is only cross-boot deterministic under a pinned config, and gates 2 and 3 compare a baseline server against a candidate server -- two processes. Without the pins the gate fires on boot noise instead of on the patch. This is the one structural difference from the llama.cpp arena, where an ordinary serve command is already cross-boot identical.
pinnedServeConfig.measured: 2026-07-28, Qwen3.6-27B-NVFP4 on vLLM 0.26.0, three boots each: identical across boots with --enforce-eager AND with cudagraphs on. So capture is not the cause and the arena does NOT have to pay eager execution. Supersedes the 2026-07-27 five-boot finding, which used --max-num-seqs 4.
pins: --max-num-seqs 1  (prime suspect for the earlier cross-boot failure: it sets the profiling batch shape, and batch shape already flips the argmax on this part at n=2)
--kv-cache-memory-bytes  (so the KV pool is not sized from profiled free memory, which changes block count and therefore attention tiling)

determinism.batchSize: 12/12 identical at batch 1 warm; n=2 -> 2 distinct, n=6 -> 5. Any batching breaks token identity, so the ranked track is serial.
determinism.crossBoot: Holds under the pinned config above (3/3 boots). Does not hold without it.

thermalGate.note: The Spark idles ~43 C and a measured arm heats it ~10 C, repeatably. mlxfast's fixed 40 C is unreachable here.

multiNode.why: Not yet. Whether greedy token identity survives an NCCL allreduce is UNMEASURED -- two attempts on 2026-07-28 died on 'RPC call to sample_tokens timed out' before producing an answer, for reasons unrelated to determinism. Until that is settled no TP target can be ranked, because the cheap gate would be comparing across a collective whose reduction order is not known to be stable.
multiNode.intent: Multi-node IS in scope for this arena -- plenty of Spark owners have two or more, and the clustered recipes are the ones that most need kernel help.

policy.optimizationVsRecipe: Optimizations preserve output and get the cheap gate. Changes that alter output (precision, quantization, sampling, speculation) are a new RECIPE on howtospark.com, not an arena submission, and need eval evidence.
policy.configVsEngine: Tuning serve FLAGS is a recipe, not a submission. This arena ranks changes to what the engine DOES with a fixed config -- dispatch, kernel selection, memory layout, scheduling.
